## &#127914; Sages & Tricksters {.smaller}

\

### Setup
- Draw one card from the envelope. Keep it hidden.
- **Black = Sage.** You always tell the truth.
- **Red = Trickster.** You always lie.
- The six cards are printed on the envelope. **Count the red ones** --- that is
  how many Tricksters your group has.
- The **fact** on the slip is true.

### Goal
Work out who is which. Everyone is on the same side, including the Tricksters.

## &#128260; How to play {.smaller}

  /* Top right: reveal's controls and progress bar sit along the bottom edge,

### 1. Questions --- two rounds
- Each round, **every player asks one** yes/no question about the cards.
- **Everyone answers**, about their own card.
- Sages answer truthfully. Tricksters always answer falsely.

### 2. Debate
- Compare answers. Look for contradictions.
- You may **not** say which card you hold, or which role you are.

### 3. Conclusion
- Agree on everyone's roles, then reveal.

<details class="hint-pop">
<summary>&#129535; Asking well</summary>
<div class="pop-body">
<ul>
<li>Ask about a <strong>card</strong> &mdash; its suit, or its rank.</li>
<li>Asking about a card's <strong>colour</strong> is allowed. Try it and see what happens.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>

::: notes
Click "Asking well" bottom right when you are ready, or leave it shut.

"Is your card red?" gets no from everyone; "is your card black?" gets yes from
everyone. Say only that colour questions are a trap, not why --- let them
predict it. Hold the real method back: if a group stalls, hint that two
properties which cannot both be true of one card will do it.
:::

## What did you just do? {.activity}

You settled on an answer without being told it.

Write down the step that convinced you:

\

"I knew \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ was a Trickster because \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_."

{{< countdown minutes=3 >}}

::: notes
Collect two or three. Nearly all take the form: if they were a Sage, then X and
not-X. Do not name it yet.
:::

## What just happened {.smaller}

\

You never saw a role.

\

You checked what people said against the **six cards everyone could see**.

\

Some answers could not be true of any of them. Those were the liars.

::: notes
The six cards are public, so every answer is checkable against them. A Trickster
inverts, so sooner or later they claim something no card in the envelope
supports. That is the contradiction the debate round is hunting for.
:::

## Lying is an operator {.smaller}

Let $1$ mean yes and $0$ mean no.

```{=html}
<style>
  table.xor{border-collapse:collapse; margin:0.2em auto 0 auto; font-size:1.05em;}
  table.xor th, table.xor td{border:1px solid #95A5A6; padding:0.22em 0.9em; text-align:center;}
  /* Quarto rewrites <th> to <td data-quarto-table-cell-role="th">, so target both */
  table.xor th,
  table.xor td[data-quarto-table-cell-role="th"]{background:#ECF0F1; font-size:0.72em;
    font-weight:700; color:#2C3E50;}
  table.xor colgroup{display:none;}
  table.xor tr.alive td{background:#FDEDEC; font-weight:700; color:#C0392B;}
  table.xor tr.alive td:last-child{border-right:4px solid #C0392B;}
</style>
```

:::: columns
::: {.column width="44%"}

```{=html}
<table class="xor">
<tr><th>your card<br>has it</th><th>you<br>lie</th><th>you<br>say</th></tr>
<tr><td>0</td><td>0</td><td>0</td></tr>
<tr class="alive"><td>0</td><td>1</td><td>1</td></tr>
<tr class="alive"><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>1</td></tr>
<tr><td>1</td><td>1</td><td>0</td></tr>
</table>
```

:::

::: {.column width="56%"}

You hear **1**.

::: {.fragment}
Two rows fit. Nothing so far separates them.
:::

::: {.fragment}
To kill one, you must **fix one of the input columns**.
:::

::: {.fragment}
You cannot fix **you lie** --- that is the thing you are hunting.
:::

::: {.fragment}
So fix **your card has it**.
:::

::: {.fragment}
\

**What could you ask that would do that?**
:::

:::
::::

::: notes
Drive the discussion from the table. Walk down the right column one reveal at a
time and let them supply the last step.

The answer they should reach: ask about a property whose value you already know
for that person --- then the "has it" column is fixed, only two rows remain, and
those two differ in the output. So the answer they give reports the lie bit
directly.

**Either value works.** Fix the column to 0 and the top two rows survive, so a
"yes" means lying. Fix it to 1 and the bottom two survive, so a "no" means
lying. If a group offers one direction, ask for the other.

In practice known-false is much easier to find. After a "yes" the surviving
cards are (black with the property) together with (red without it) --- a set
spanning both colours. Naming a suit or rank none of them has is easy; finding
something a mixed bag all share is rare. Across eight packets there were 20
known-false follow-ups available and 1 known-true. Worth asking why, if someone
notices.

Do not name XOR. The Truth slide introduces the same four-row shape for OR, and
naming it there lands better.

Later in the term, the direction is the point: a truth table is normally read
left to right, inputs to output. All hour they read it right to left. That is
what you do with data --- you see what came out and argue about what went in.
:::

## Two claims {.activity}

\

**A.** Seat 3 is a Trickster.

**B.** Students who come to tutorials do better on examlets.

\

What would it take to **settle** each one?

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
A: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
B: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_
:::
:::::

{{< countdown minutes=4 >}}

::: notes
Deliberately from different domains. If both came from the card game it would
look like a fact about card games.
:::

## Two claims {.smaller}

|  | **A.** Seat 3 is a Trickster | **B.** Tutorials help |
|---|---|---|
| The claim is about | six people, in this room | all students, including ones not here yet |
| Can you examine every case? | **yes** | **no** |
| So the method is | check them all | sample, and generalise |
| Verdict | **settled** | **supported** |
| Being wrong means | you made an error | you were unlucky |

\

Both are inference. The method follows from the information --- not the other
way round.

::: notes
The discriminator is whether the evidence reaches as far as the claim does.
Exact inference is not a different mental operation; it is what inference
becomes when the domain is small enough to exhaust.

This course is the left-hand column. Most of their degree is the right. Do not
oversell it yet --- lecture 3 earns it, when the same cereal claim is asked
first of a dataset and then of every cereal ever manufactured.
:::

# Logic

## Truth {.activity}

Make at least 3 observations about the following table:

::::: columns
::: {.column width="30%"}

| $p$ | $q$ | $p \lor q$ |
|---|---|:--------:|
| F | F |   F    |
| F | T |   T    |
| T | F |   T    |
| T | T |   T    |

:::

::: {.column width="70%"}

*

\

*

\

*

:::
:::::

{{< countdown minutes=5 >}}

## Summary

::::: columns
::: {.column width="30%"}

| $p$ | $q$ | $p \lor q$ |
|---|---|:--------:|
| F | F |   F    |
| F | T |   T    |
| T | F |   T    |
| T | T |   T    |

:::

::: {.column style="width: 70%; font-size: 80%;"}

*   The diagram is a _Truth Table_
*   $p$, $q$ are _variables_ taking one of two _Boolean_ values (T/F, 1/0)
*   $\lor$ is a _binary operator_: a function from 2 Boolean inputs to 1 Boolean output, characterized by its output column
*   $\lor$ corresponds to the English _or_
*   $p \lor q$ is a _proposition_

:::
:::::

## Cool down {.activity}

*   How many rows for a proposition on 3 variables? On $k$?

\

*   Name an operator taking 1 variable: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

\

*   Name an operator taking 3 variables: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

\

*   How many different binary operators could there be?

{{< countdown minutes=5 >}}

::: notes
$2^k$ rows. $2^{2^k}$ operators on $k$ variables; 16 binary ones. Half the binary
operators are commutative (8).
:::
